utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Mathias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant, Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom; the Registrar, the usher, the legal officers, and the interpreters in the booths, as well as the technicians. If I always ask for the appearances, this is because there may be people following the proceedings, there may be people in the gallery or following the proceedings via internet, and this helps them to know the names of the people present in the courtroom. As I have already said, as I said yesterday, the Trial Chamber has to render its decision on certification. The Trial Chamber certifies the decision concerning -- the motion for certification dated the 4th October 2004. It was filed by Defence counsel, but this only concerns the following points: (d), (e), and (f) that were mentioned in paragraphs -- in paragraph 3 of the said motion. The Trial Chamber is not hereby certifying the appeal for (a), (b), (c), and (j) in paragraph 3. A written decision will soon be produced by the Registrar in which our oral decision will be explained in further detail. I believe that the Defence has some submissions to make with regard to the witnesses who will be heard here. So you may take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. I would first like to make sure you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, say da, say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. And before you take the solemn declaration, I would be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zijad Caber. I was born in January 1958 in Travnik in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession, or what current position do you hold? And what was your profession or what post did you hold in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At present, I'm employed in the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am the head of the field office with its headquarters in Travnik. In 1993, I was the commander of 312th Brigade with its headquarters in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you work with the Ministry of Defence, you must have a rank. What rank do you hold in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that I'm now a civil servant, I do not hold a rank now, in view of my present post. However, when I was serving in the army of the Federation, my rank was that of brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you had the rank of general within the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you prefer that I address you as general or as "sir"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As "sir."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you inform the Trial Chamber -- could you tell the Trial Chamber whether you have already testified in international proceedings or in local proceedings in your country, or is this the first time you're testifying before a court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now ask Madam Usher to show you a document which contains the text of the solemn declaration. Could you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Before Defence counsel commences its examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with certain explications about how we will proceed here. You have just taken the solemn declaration and you have said you will speak the truth and nothing but the truth. This means that it is your duty to answer the questions put to you, and you must answer them truthfully. In the case of false testimony, you could be given a sentence. You could be punished by a sentence, a prison sentence. When a witness makes statements to the Trial Chamber, according to the Rules, what the witness says can't be used against him in subsequent proceedings that could be instituted against him. The witness has a sort of immunity in relation to the witness's testimony. You've just taken the solemn declaration which means that you are a witness who will be testifying in the interests of justice, although you have been called as a Defence witness because you only belong to the Defence in that you must answer their questions. The Defence will conduct its examination-in-chief, after which the Prosecution will cross-examine you, and the three Judges sitting before you may ask you questions at any point in time if they believe that this could clarify some of the answers that you have provided to the parties, or if the Judges believe that, in order to establish truth, it is necessary to put further questions to you in order to fill any gaps. If the Judges do put questions to you, both parties have the right to ask you additional questions. This is how we have proceeded so far in the case of Prosecution witnesses, and we will proceed in the same manner in the case of Defence witnesses. The principles in force must be the same for everyone. If you encounter any difficulties when a question is put to you, do inform us of the fact. We are here to deal with any difficulties that may arise. Try to understand the questions as best as possible, and if you fail to understand the question ask the person putting it to you to rephrase the question. As you may be aware, the proceedings are oral proceedings, and it is your testimony that will be transcribed. There will be a written document of your testimony, and then the Defence could present new documents or mention documents that have already been tendered so that we could compare questions posed with given documents. The evidence that the Defence presents could then be admitted through you as a witness. Roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding. We'll be following the same procedure we have followed so far whenever a witness was called to testify. Without wasting any more time, though we still have some time left before we have the break, I will give the floor to the Defence now and they will commence their examination-in-chief. But I would also like to point out that after the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic has concluded its examination-in-chief, the Defence team for Mr. Kubura may also ask you some questions. If they believe it is necessary, they may ask you questions that relate to their Defence strategy. And then it is the right of the Prosecution to cross-examine you. I now turn to General Hadzihasanovic's Defence who will now commence with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Caber. Before I start putting questions to you, I will ask you to observe some instructions I will now give you. You and I speak the same language, and when I put my question to you, you are in a position to answer immediately. However, your testimony before this Trial Chamber is such that others in the courtroom must be able to understood what we are saying. That is why I wish to ask you as soon as I finish putting my question, would you please wait a little until you hear in your headset that the interpretation has been completed, and then you can begin to answer the question. The interpreters have a duty to convey everything we are saying faithfully, and they will tell us when we fail to observe this rule. Did you understand this, Mr. Caber?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already told the President what your name is and when you were born. Could you please tell me where you were born.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I was born in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Travnik is in Central Bosnia, about 90 kilometres to the northwest of Sarajevo. Going from Banja Luka to the southeast, it's 140 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you live until the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: From my birth until the beginning of the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather until the beginning of the war: I lived in Travnik until 1976. And then when I graduated from the military academy in Belgrade, from 1980 onwards I worked in various towns in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what schools did you finish?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: In Travnik, I completed the secondary technical school; and from 1976 to 1980, I attended the military academy in Belgrade for the ground forces. And my stream was armoured and mechanised units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your duty in the JNA, and did you hold any rank?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: While I was employed in the JNA, I was platoon leader, company leader, and in 1990 I was the commander of an armoured battalion in Dugo Selo near Zagreb. The rank I had was captain first-class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, did you leave the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. At my own request, I left the JNA in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the reasons why you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The reasons were the following: The idea with which I embarked, first on my military education and then my military career as an officer in the former JNA, that idea was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the JNA, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I went to my native town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the situation you found when you arrived in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: In Travnik, there was a post-election atmosphere. Multiparty elections had been held, and these had given rise to political parties. I kept coming across these through my contacts with fellow citizens and friends, and one could see that ethnicity was more important than it had been before on my previous visits to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what parties in Travnik entered the government after the elections?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Action and the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the makeup of the population was in the town itself and how this population lived before the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: In the town of Travnik, the population reflected the makeup of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole. For the most part, the majority were Muslims, Bosniaks, followed by Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Before these multiparty elections, people lived together as friends and neighbours. And up until that time, I had never even known who was a Serb, who was a Croat, and who was a Muslim by ethnicity. That year was when I began to notice these differences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the town of Travnik, what other territory belongs to Travnik Municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Travnik Municipality is quite fragmented. There are two river valleys, and we referred to them as the Lasva River Valley which encompasses the villages along the banks of the River Lasva, from Karaula to the point where the leaves Travnik in the direction of Vitez. And then the other part is the Bila River, which encompasses villages on the southern slopes of Mount Vlasic and along the banks of the River Bila as far as the border of the Municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, could you please indicate on the map you have before you the area you have described. First, let me ask you, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I do. I'm fully familiar with it. The Municipality of Travnik with its seat in the town of Travnik here. I have just mentioned the area around the River Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can what the witness is saying be shown on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The River Lasva flows by Travnik or through Travnik, and then flows on toward Vitez. And on this axis, what is characteristic is this area here, referred to as Karaula. This is a cluster of villages which have connections with both Serb, Muslim, and Croatian areas. And above this Karaula valley, there is a plateau of Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is Vlasic, Mr. Caber?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: It's a mountain. And its highest peak was and is Paljenik where there is a radio relay station, and its height is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the height.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This other area connected to Travnik Municipality along the River Bila. The villages go from Gluha Bubarica, Orahovo, Dube, Vaslic, Mehurici, Han Bila, and then this is linked up with the road leading to Vitez, and another road which is not as good, a macadam road going to the Municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. When you arrived in Travnik, did you have a job, and did somebody offer you a post at one point, or a duty?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As I had voluntarily left the former JNA, I was unemployed. With the help of friends from the town and following their suggestion, I asked for a post where I could work as a former professional soldier, and I was offered the job in -- a job in the Territorial Defence of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which party in power did the post of commander of the municipal staff belong, and what other party held the other posts important for defence?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The two key positions - I don't want to go into the municipal posts any further in relation to defence - the HDZ had the post of secretariat for national defence, the municipal secretariat. And the task of the secretariat was recruitment and mobilisation, calling up the reserve forces at the request of the municipal staff. The SDA had the post of commander of Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who elected you to the post of commander of the Territorial Defence municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: This was quite a lengthy procedure. The SDA nominated me, and I was appointed by the commander of the republican TO staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this happen and until when did you hold the post of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commander of the municipal TO staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: These activities took place in September 1991 and went on until October 1991 when I was appointed as commander of the TO staff. I remained at that post until the end of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What further duties did you have in the Territorial Defence, or rather, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina until the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Later on, I was chief of staff of the Territorial Defence in Travnik Municipality, until November 1992, when I was appointed commander of the 312th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, in order to establish the facts, could you please tell us briefly what the Territorial Defence represented in the system of defence of the former SFRY and the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Within the armed forces of the former SFRY, its components were the former JNA and the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence was the armed force that was linked to the socialist republics which provided the equipment and materiel for the units of the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence as such, as its very name tells us, was closely linked to the territory of a municipality or several municipalities depending on the tasks it was assigned by the higher command, such as the district staffs or the republican staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When as a young officer of the JNA you took over the post of commander in the Territorial Defence, did you have any special knowledge of the structure and activity of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: No, not to begin with. However, this all boiled down to organising the work and the establishment of the wartime units in the Territorial Defence. I knew about that, but I did not have an opportunity to work with such units because they never developed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In line with the regulations then in force when you were appointed commander, can you tell us who was in charge of Defence and whether the commander of the TO staff was a member of the civil authorities, or rather of the wartime presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence had its chain of command going up to the republican staff, or rather the republic, the broader social and political community. The then commander of the TO staff had links to the municipality and the municipal services because it was the municipality that financed the work of the peacetime staff of the Territorial Defence, and the materiel and equipment were provided by the citizens and the enterprises of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you took over this duty in 1991, who did you find in the Territorial Defence staff, and what was its ethnic composition compared to the ethnic composition of the town?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: When I took over this duty, there were two of us who were Bosniaks; three were Serbs; and there were five Croats. That was the peacetime staff. And these were people who were professionally employed in the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, you just said that the municipality and the republic provided the funds for the purchase of equipment and materiel for Territorial Defence units. When you were appointed commander of the staff, what kind of equipment and materiel did you find there and were you able to make use of these weapons freely?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: While I was still a member of the former JNA, I knew that the then Yugoslav authorities had issued an order that weapons should be confiscated from the Territorial Defence staffs and put under control in the barracks of the former JNA. And that's what I found when I arrived in Travnik. The weapons of the Territorial Defence of which I was the head was stored in buildings guarded by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time when you took over your duties, did you observe some persons turning up in Travnik who had previously taken part in the hostilities in the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As I've already said, in the Republic of Croatia the conflict had already started. And one of the reasons I left was that this same JNA was attacking citizens of the same country, and that's one of the reasons I left. Probably under the influence of ethnic affiliation, citizens of Croat ethnicity in 1991 went to Croatia, and together with their friends and relatives, took part in the defence against the attacks and the aggression by the former JNA. These same persons then returned home to Travnik with a wealth of experience, wartime experience, if we can say that; to carry weapons or other equipment constitutes wartime experience, or being part of a military unit in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you could sometimes see these people carrying weapons and wearing uniforms even before the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what I was trying to say. These were armed groups of men who had taken part honourably in the defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, while you were performing your duties, was Bosnia and Herzegovina declared an independent state and Herzegovina declared an independent state and recognised as such?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the fact that these were topical issues at the time, Bosnia and Herzegovina gained its independence, first of all through a referendum on joining the European Community of Independent States. I remember this was on the 6th of April when Bosnia and Herzegovina gained its independence, and there were various political repercussions that followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As commander of the Territorial Defence, did you know that the Presidency of the country had issued a decision in connection with the armed forces of the newly recognised state; and if so, what was this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: This is a good question. I remember that there were quite a few various armed formations, and I'm referring to groups of armed men present at the time. The Presidency, alluding to the assessments made by the Ministry of the Interior and other bodies, decided that all these armed groups who might cause unpleasantness for the citizens should be placed under a single command, a command of all the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the Territorial Defence. And I think this happened on the 8th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When an imminent threat of war was declared by the Presidency, did the Territorial Defence staff have any possibility of carrying out and implementing the defence plans that had been prepared in peacetime should there be a war or an imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: When I took over my duty, I received a metal safe containing well-thought-out and detailed plans for the mobilisation of all the armed forces - I'm referring to the units under the command of the Territorial Defence - in case of war, mobilisation and the forming of units. I opened the safe and looked at those documents, and closed it again because there was no chance of implementing any of that. Why? Because the people who belonged to the Croatian nation did not want to enter the Territorial Defence. Unfortunately, most Serbs, and I won't go into this in detail, had either left together with the former JNA or through certain channels had already obtained weapons. I'm referring to citizens of Serb ethnicity. And they were -- they had links to Serbian forces. We did not know what the plans were of the Serbs, Croats, or Bosniaks. We just had battalions and detachments with certain professional qualifications and professional personnel. That's what we had in view. It was very hard. On the 20th of April, I remember well there was an attack on Turbe, which is a part of Travnik Municipality, by the Serb forces with a formation that belonged to the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, as an officer of the former JNA, you must have known that some men of military age were to be mobilised into the JNA. What happened in Travnik Municipality to these men who were according to the previous plans reservists of the JNA? Did they remain?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: There were reserve units of the Territorial Defence staff comprising certain citizens. There were also reserve units of the then JNA in the Travnik area. And citizens who belonged to those units, whether wartime or operational, these men were nowhere. These citizens could not become part of what the Territorial Defence was doing in wartime, and these were small units. The republican TO staff, pursuant to previous orders, had been reduced in size. In the 1970s, there was a large number of units, but this was reduced to a very small number so that we only actually had two detachments in the staff. Everything else was part of the operative wartime units of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, a minute ago you said that the position of the secretary of the secretariat for national defence whose task was to recruit and mobilise men was a position held by an HDZ member. Can you remember the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He's a friend of mine to this very day. Tomo Rajic held that position. He held the position of the secretary of the secretariat for national defence in Travnik. And at the beginning, in cooperation with me, he told me that his hair stood on end when he asked himself what he should do because we were not prepared for what was to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the secretary of the secretariat for national defence attempt to mobilise all the citizens of Travnik, the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats? Did he attempt to mobilise them and have them become members of the Territorial Defence which was the only legitimate force in the country?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: He did try to do this, but the situation in the field was such, and I have already mentioned the breakup of the system, the one that had been prepared before, but the decisions of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina on placing all armed formations under the TO command, Mr. Rajic and myself appealled to the citizens over the radio. We followed an inverse order. We made a public appeal, and we asked all the citizens of Travnik Municipality from local communes to the Municipality of Travnik, we appealled to them to report to units of the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that appeal, apart from that appeal, was there a significant number of Croats who organised themselves into quite different military formations?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well, with regard to these appeals, it's interesting that in some of the rural or village areas, the Croat people did stand by the Croatian army, the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council. That didn't bother me at the time, but some townspeople did sign documents saying they wanted to be members of the staff, or rather of the Travnik TO. This was the most regular and legitimate armed force in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the forces of the Croatian people then? Who was the commander of the HVO, as you say?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: At the time, it was the HVO leadership who later formed their own government. I really wouldn't go into the details now. I wouldn't really go into the names of these people. There were quite a few of them who were in positions of responsibility, who armed men, who had contact with the higher organs of power outside of Travnik as well. But on the whole, one felt that there was a parallel military presence in the Municipality of Travnik as far as the Territorial Defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This newly formed HVO, was it resubordinated -- or was it subordinated to you as the TO commander?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: No, at no point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, what was your attitude towards the fact that a completely different military force appeared in the town?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As a professional, I was probably glad of the fact that we had what we did have in the field because at those joint meetings, and I'm talking about the wartime Presidency, if we're talking about the beginning of the aggression as of the 20th of April, we already had certain problems at our forward edge facing the Serbian forces because we had to defend ourselves from the Serbs with hunting rifles, et cetera. And in other areas, we had problems that had more to do with the political structures. But we did have a presence there, and we did try to resolve problems by finding various types of solutions. We decided to form a common staff, a joint staff, joint command, joint units of various kinds. At the meetings, there were some quite nice agreements. But in the field, the agreements that had been reached in offices or sometimes even in the field were never actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just mentioned hunting rifles, et cetera, and a minute ago you mentioned the fact that the Territorial Defence had a significant amount of weapons, that the BH Republic and the Municipality -- and in the Municipality of Travnik they had been obtaining for a number of years. You said that these weapons had been placed under JNA control. Where were these weapons located, and did the JNA return these weapons to you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat this: The TO weapons, the weapons of the citizens of Travnik Municipality were under the control of the former JNA in a Muslim facility which was in the immediate vicinity of the town centre. The JNA provided security for these weapons, and while they were located in the territory of the municipality, the JNA secured these weapons and didn't allow them to be taken when the mobilisation was implemented. We had a Serbian attack on the 22nd of April, and the situation was chaotic. We defended ourselves to an extent with the weapons of the police force and to an extent the weapons obtained on the black market by citizens. Above all, these weapons were automatic rifles. They came from Croatia, and a rifle cost between a thousand and a thousand two hundred German marks at the time. People had their own weapons. For their own personal security, they obtained them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly: The JNA did not return those weapons to you. What happened to those weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: No, they didn't return the weapons, but those weapons, since being present in the Travnik -- in Travnik did not suit them, the barracks was in the centre of the town -- since this did not suit them, they announced that departure in the direction of the Serbian force who were surrounding the area and were at the front in the direction of the Municipality of Travnik. They announced their departure. This was at the beginning of May. And that night, they had prepared the weapons. They blew up the warehouses, the equipment, the weapons, and we were left without our weapons, the weapons of citizens, the weapons of the workers who lived in Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is perhaps the right time for a break since after these introductory remarks on the situation in Travnik, I will be moving on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, is there anything you would like to say, or are you getting up because of the pause, because of the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could just briefly, Mr. President, I noted that quite a number of the questions that my colleague put to the witness were leading questions, and I didn't object primarily because this was background and historical matter. But I'm just stating that -- I don't want to break up the flow of her presentation, but once we get into the time frame of the indictment I will certainly be objecting to each and every question that's leading, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yesterday I thought about reminding the parties of these principles. When the Prosecution witnesses came, whenever there was a leading question, Defence counsel objected. So let's try to avoid having such objections again. Try to conduct your examination in accordance with the rules in force. In the course of your examination-in-chief, the question you put should be a neutral one, and the witness will answer your question. It's only when we get to the cross-examination that everything is allowed. Those are the rules, and we have to respect them. It is 20 to 4.00, and we will resume at 10 past 4.00 after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the usher call the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're in open session now. And the witness will be called back into the courtroom so that we can continue with the examination-in-chief. You may take the floor to continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue examining the witness, I would like to ask the usher to show the witness a series of documents prepared by the Defence. And before the beginning of the trial, we provided these documents to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution. So could these documents please be handed over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, before the break you mentioned the fact that parallel organs of power had been established. Could you now please have a look at part 2 in this series of documents, and it is entitled "the HVO," the Croatian Defence Council. And could you have a look at documents under number 1, number 2, and number 3. But first of all, could you tell me whether you have located the document.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is a decision on appointing a president and deputy president of the municipal HVO council. Mr. Caber, at that time, at the time this decision was taken, were you aware of the fact that the persons mentioned in this decision were appointed to the positions referred to in the decision?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I can see the decision. I have the decision before me, and I know these people. I know Nenad Zec and Pero Krizanac personally. And it's true that at this time, a parallel government was formed. It was for the Croatian people. It was the HVO for Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, what happened to the Croatian members of the wartime Presidency after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will interrupt you at this point because we can't find the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at the end of these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue then

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, could you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to the HDZ representatives in the wartime presidency of the Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The members of the parallel organs of power in the HVO Municipality of Travnik left the wartime presidency, and we in fact had two organs of power in Travnik Municipality. We had the HVO of Travnik Municipality, and we had the legal municipal organ. That is to say, we had the wartime presidency headed by the president of the Municipal Assembly of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, this HVO presidency, or rather, the HDZ in Travnik, did they express their view of who the legal authorities in Travnik were?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: These documents refresh my memory. As I was already working in the Territorial Defence staff, I knew from my contacts with certain commanders of the HVO that the Croatian people at that time, in 1992 - and later, but that is immaterial now - felt that the HVO of Travnik Municipality was the only legitimate authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at Document Number 2. It's some minutes. And there is a conclusion. Does the conclusion under number 1 reflect what you knew in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. From that date, it says here it was the 5th of September, on the territory of Travnik Municipality for the Croatian people, it was only the HVO government that existed and no other. And Muslims could take part in it with 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any changes in the areas of the judiciary and the police force?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. As soon as you set up a government, you want to have the judiciary and executive powers in your control so that a judiciary was set up, and an HVO police, and this was in parallel to the other police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at Document Number 3. These are conclusions. And under number 1, does this correspond to the facts and to what you knew in 1992 about the events in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. I have no further comment to make. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Caber, could you please tell me now what was the combat situation in Travnik Municipality, and what was the position of the Territorial Defence at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As I said, when talking about the wartime composition of the Territorial Defence in early April 1992, of the manpower reported, we formed units on the territory of Travnik Municipality. We formed detachments according to the territorial principle and district staffs or area staffs in those parts of the municipality where there was more than one detachment, where there were at least two detachments in order to facilitate communications and command and control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. You've already explained this. But my question was, were there any combat activities and with what forces attacking Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As I've already said, on the 20th of April, the Serb forces started taking parts of Travnik Municipality. And with all the forces and all the equipment we had, and this was very meagre, very modest, we attempted to stop them, and we did stop the Serb forces which were far superior in terms of weaponry at the line in Turbe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is Turbe compared to the centre of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well, in relation to the centre of Travnik, let me show you. This is Turbe. This is the Turbe area. And in relation to Travnik, it's about 8 kilometres away from the centre of Travnik. In Turbe, we had a population that to the north of Turbe comprised Croatian villages, and to the west of Turbe there were Serb villages. To the south were Muslim or Bosniak villages. The forces of our TO detachment securing this line were here, to prevent the Serb forces from advancing further into Travnik Municipality. It's noteworthy that the HVO participated with a small part of their forces where the Croatian villages were, together with us, but not under our command on the southern slopes of Mount Vlasic in the area of the village of Dijaci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I think the situation is a little clearer now. As I said, I do apologise. This is not a question. I was just summing up what the witness just said. Practically now, the line was approximately 8 kilometres from Travnik. Tell us, please, in the town of Travnik itself, what kind of changes took place? Did some people arrive in Travnik in the period between the spring and the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: In 1992, Travnik Municipality was of interest to the international public and international media. What had happened in the Bosnian Krajina - better to say in Prijedor, Banja Luka, Kozarac - all the population, mostly Muslim but also in part Croatian, starting in May began to arrive every ten days or so, and especially in July and August 1992. There would be over 15.000 refugees in Travnik in a single day from the Bosnian Krajina and from the municipalities that were then part of Jajce in the direction of Vrbac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area of your municipality, were there other armed clashes apart from what you just mentioned in Turbe, and did this have any effect on the overall situation in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: On the Vlasic plateau, I didn't indicate that. There were also Serb forces exerting pressure, threatening to take over the municipality. And this was very intensive in the summer. The front line toward the Serb forces stretched out for over 70 kilometres, viewed tactically, in terms of the defence lines held by the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period of time while all this fighting was going on and while all these problems were there, were there any changes in the regulations governing the armed forces and what bearing did this have on your position as commander of the Territorial Defence staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As far as regulations and legislation go concerning the work of the armed forces, up to the beginning of the aggression and throughout most of the month of May, we implemented the former regulations of the Former Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The then presidency enacted laws and regulations about the work of the Territorial Defence staff and the members of the Territorial Defence. And then these were implemented to govern our work, discipline, and everything else that the documents covered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until the end of 1992, was this situation regarding the large number of refugees complicated by other events which had an effect on the functioning of the Territorial Defence staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As I said, the HVO units which were present in the town of Travnik as well as in other municipalities, and especially the parallel government bodies in Travnik, made it impossible for the legitimate authorities to operate normally, not to mention the normal operation of the Territorial Defence staff, with respect to defending the town from Serb forces, equipping our units with equipment and materiel, which was very scarce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any conflicts in your immediate surroundings; and if so, did they have any bearing on the situation in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: By that time, I was chief of staff of the municipal TO staff, and in June 1992 there had already been incidents and conflicts in the neighbouring municipality of Novi Travnik, Vitez, Gornji Vakuf, and these arose because of certain so-called misunderstandings. That's why there were conflicts between the armed forces of both the TO and the HVO. All this had an impact on the soldiers of the Territorial Defence because they had friends and relatives in neighbouring municipalities. And their basic task was to defend the town of Travnik from the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, who did the representatives of the HVO try to blame for the conflicts in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well, they always blamed members of, as they call them, the Muslim forces, the Muslim government or when we were around the table of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The forces of the Territorial Defence under your command, did they at any point mount any kind of attack or cause any kind of incident to justify these accusations?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: No, not while I was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are leading questions, and I'll again do everything I can to avoid disrupting the direct. But again, with the counsel and witness speaking the same language, it's particularly difficult. But we will object to leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Residovic, if you look at the transcript, line 16:34, you will see that this really is a leading question and that Mr. Mundis's objection is justified. The question was formulated in such a way as to be strongly leading, and the witness can respond with a yes or no. Please try to formulate your questions so as to avoid this, although it's true that our Rules are a synthesis of continental and Anglo-Saxon law. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am trying very hard not to put leading questions. I would like to ask my learned friend to tell me which of my questions was a leading question so that I can avoid putting such questions in the future. It could have been a problem of interpretation, and I will ask the interpreters to interpret my question exactly as I put it. It is obvious we're having interpretation problems. Would my learned friend, Mr. Mundis, please tell me which question it was that he objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought I had explained this, but Mr. Mundis will do that now. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the English transcript, the question beginning at line 1 of page 39, which is about to disappear from the screen: "The forces of the Territorial Defence under your command, did they at any point mount any kind of attack or cause any kind of incident to justify these accusations" suggests the answer to that question, which is the classic definition of a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that the witness answered with a no, so this was then a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be more careful because in my view this was a question that made it possible for the witness to say either yes or no. However, I will take on board this objection, and I will do my best not to put similar questions in the future, even though it was not really a leading question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please now look at Document Number -- HVO number 4. I will ask you to read the first passage, the first nine lines.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: "The main issue..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can read it to yourself silently, and then please tell me, this comment in the HVO document, is this something that you knew about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in 1992? Does it correspond to your knowledge of the situation then?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before, but this event reminds me of things I knew. I knew that this sort of thing happened on the ground and that this information was correct because it was compiled by people belonging to the same forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In late 1992, did events occur to further complicate the situation in your municipality and the duties you were performing as chief of staff in that period?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The sequence of events that caused problems in Travnik was, again, the arrival of refugees from the Bosnian Krajina, the fall of Jajce into Serbian hands, as well as parts of the occupied territory of Travnik Municipality, Karaula, which I indicated on the map a little while ago. The villages around Karaula which were both Croatian and Muslim, the Muslim villages were in the majority, but these had all been taken over by the Serb forces so that there was an even greater influx of refugees into the small area of the town centre and into the neighbouring municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, at one point on the territory of your municipality, were certain military formations emerging composed of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: When we go back in time, in June of that year, the people who had arrived from the Bosnian Krajina formed a battalion, a Krajina battalion, and this battalion together with the refugees was in the barracks in Travnik. Right after that, another unit arrived, the 7th Krajina Brigade. It arrived in Travnik, and they also settled in the Travnik barracks. Later on, pursuant to orders, they became the 17th Krajina Brigade in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, apart from these armed forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the units of the Territorial Defence, the units formed from refugees, the HVO, at that time in Travnik were there any other units not belonging to any other military establishment?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: It's true that the Ministry of the Interior, the then civilian police, had its reserve force which they armed and equipped with long barrels. And at that time, in the summer and autumn of 1992, we also saw the formation of a small Muslim force, probably under the auspices of what the -- or rather, because the HVO had set up Croatian forces, these people were inspired to create Muslim forces consisting of citizens of Travnik Municipality, and they had a certain code which was linked to the religion they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already said that you had no superior role in -- toward the HVO. Did the units and Territorial Defence staff, were they superior to the police forces and to the newly established Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, did you hear the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, in view of the objection raised by my learned friend, would you please tell me over which units did you have a command responsibility? Which units were under your command?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The units of the municipal Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Territorial Defence units include the armed forces of the police?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, did the Territorial Defence units also comprise the unit of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no. I do know that they were there, that they had contacts with the commander of the TO staff. But as far as I can recall, they were under the direct command -- no, they were not under the direct command of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, please tell me, did at some point in late 1992 there come about a reorganisation of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Territorial Defence; and if so, when did this happen and what kind of changes took place?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: All these problems which had to do with the work of the Territorial Defence staff - the combat operations of the units under its command; the fragmentation of these units; the problems concerning unprofessional people appointed to certain duties; the problems that had to do with others who did not want to be part of the TO, although we had a common enemy; all this led to the fact that in November 1992, a group of officers headed by Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic spent some time in Travnik. It could also have been in late October. Jajce had fallen. Karaula had fallen. A lot of things were going on, so I'm not sure about the date any more. But in any case, it was either November or October. And they were given the task by the supreme command of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to establish brigades in Travnik Municipality and further afield and to establish a corps with headquarters in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember what brigades were supposed to be established on the territory of Travnik Municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Two brigades. The 306th Mountain Brigade and the 312th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you assume a position in one of those brigades?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I was recommended and later appointed as commander of the 312th Motorised Brigade which started operating in that capacity in November. On the 25th of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the men who composed your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The brigade was composed of former detachments of the Territorial Defence who were within the TO staff, but from the access I indicated a while ago, there was Karaula, Turbe, the core part of the town. So there were from these detachments. It was these detachments that the 312th Motorised Brigade was formed of. I would also like to point out that when I was requested to assume this position in the motorised brigade, I didn't find this acceptable as a soldier, but such was the order and it was necessary to implement the order and use the men and equipment that we had and the men who were already engaged in contact [as interpreted]. It was necessary to form a brigade somewhere in the rear in free territory, and afterwards we were supposed to return to territory where we were to be present and have a brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me where were the members of your brigade located, where they were billeted.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As far as the combat zone is concerned, the Turbe battlefield, that's where the brigade was located. The other men weren't billeted in barracks, but we would let people go on leave. We let them go home to have a rest with their families. And as far as rest is concerned, they would go to the centre of the town or in the direction of Bile, to Mehurici, to Han Bila, to Zenica, the wider Zenica area. They would go to Kakanj, Novi Travnik, and to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of equipment did your brigade have at the beginning of 1993? And I'm referring primarily to weapons.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The equipment and the weapons that the brigade had took over from TO units was very modest. We didn't have much -- we didn't have many weapons, but with respect to the strength of the brigade - that now consisted of about 3.000 men - this depended on the unit. We had a strength of 30 to 40 per cent, and they had infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of your brigade was the motorised brigade. At the time, did you have all the essential equipment that was needed to make that brigade a motorised brigade? And at any time in 1993, did you really become -- did you really become, did you reach the level that a motorised brigade should actually have?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As I've already said, a motorised brigade according to my experience as a soldier from before should have materiel equipment so that it can be mobile and carry out manoeuvres and carry out tasks. Unfortunately, we didn't have such equipment. And the title was the "motorised brigade," but in 1994 it was transformed into a mountain brigade. I can't remember the exact date, but I never managed to form a motorised brigade in accordance with what had been requested of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, I can see that you mentioned something here. You said that there were about 3.000 men. That's what appears in the transcript. Did you say 3.000 or 2.000? How many men were there in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: About 3.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the deployment of the men in a wider area from Kakanj to Zenica and as far as Travnik, could you tell me what sort of problems you had to confront as far as control and command was concerned.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I had a really difficult role to play as far as the brigade is concerned. And when it's a matter of a brigade going into combat action at the battlefield or at the front facing the Serbian forces, given all the problems in the rear in December, I already had to confront a fierce attack launched by the Serbs. And my right wing was threatened, and in fact we lost some of the territory. And all of this meant that we needed reserve forces, we needed forces which had to be brought in from the depth. And when I say "the depth," I'm actually saying they were on leave. We had to get these forces back and we had to implement our main task from the superior command, and that task was to control the territory and not to lose it. The problem was bringing these boys from the depth, and the problem was how organise the forces of the battalion that was motorised at the time and how to organise them according to establishment. We did everything -- we improvised everything, and at the time it was very hard to be a battalion commander, and especially a commander of a lower unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, you said that those men had about 30 per cent of the weapons they should have had according to establishment. Where were those weapons located? And the units that were at the front line, did they have any weapons that were held in reserve in the case of such intensive combat?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: All the weapons that the brigade had were at the forward edge in the combat zone. People would take turns to use rifles, mortars, cannons, so nothing was taken away, taken to other areas. With regard to the forward edge which had to be located in a certain area, according to the orders, the men when though went on leave went on leave without their weapons. And only in exceptional circumstances they went with their weapons, when the units were being resubordinated to a brigade from neighbouring municipalities. They would then come with their weapons and return with their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, you could probably speak at length about the problems you had to confront. But you as commander of the 312th motorised unit, did you have to confront a new problem in January, a problem that was caused by those who had been your allies until a short time before? And if so, what sort of problems did you have to confront?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992 -- that is to say, in 1993, the brigade as such had already sustained significant losses at the front edge as a result of the Serb attack. The brigade was exhausted as a result of the combat, and they were exhausted because they were hungry. We didn't have enough equipment, and this is a logistical problem. It has to do with quartermaster problems and the difficulty of obtaining food. But there was a problem that had developed in the centre of the Municipality of Travnik, and I'm referring to the organs in power. And this had to do with the declaration of the Croatian Community of Herceg Bosna. At the time, sometime in the middle of January 1993, commanders, I think one of them was Filipovic, called us from the BH Republic Army. They called on brigade commanders to inform us that as of that time, there were no legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that all the armed formations had to be placed under the command or under the rule of the HVO, that is to say -- or of the Croatian Community of Herceg Bosna. I'm sure that the Trial Chamber is familiar with these matters, so I won't go into detail. But I think that the problem became more complex when it -- dealing with my brigade and the authorities in the Travnik Municipality probably had more complex problems as a result of the refugees who continued arriving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, could you please have a look at one of the documents you have before you. The number of the document -- the title of the document is "A, Combat Report," and you can find it under number 1.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you recognise the document. Is this a document that comes from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. These are the estimates made by my staff, by my brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the introductory remarks, you mentioned what you had just stated before this Trial Chamber. Please tell me, this decision of the HVO and of the Croatian Community of Herceg Bosna, what sort of an effect did this decision have on all of you and on the combatants?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I believe that the Trial Chamber also has this document. I think everything is clear here. But what I will say is that at that time, it was very unpleasant for us in the army, and we had to think about placing ourselves under the command of an illegal entity, under the command of a parallel state that had been condemned as such. The state of Bosnia and Herzegovina that had been recognised is one that we had accepted as such, together with its organs of power, and all of a sudden something was being formed by force and we were being placed under its command. At the time, given the instructions, given the requests that had been made, I knew I had to report about the situation, and I drafted this document together with my staff. My chief of staff signed the document. We really didn't want to open a second front, to put it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've put that briefly. But what you said, is that stated in the last sentence of your document?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask you to have a look at the documents under B. The title is "movement," and the documents I'm referring to are Documents 1 to 21. And before that, before we have a look at them, I would like to ask you the following: You said you didn't want a conflict, you wanted to avoid a conflict. Did you take any measures to avoid such a conflict? Or rather, as you were in the army, did you make any efforts to calm the situation down?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I myself as a commander, my staff, and the organs of power, and in many cases the 3rd Corps that had been formed at the time and had its orders and tasks, and they asked us to make evaluations, to hold the positions facing the Serbian forces. But we were asked to do everything we could to avoid a conflict with the units and formations of the HVO. Almost on a daily basis we had contact with HVO representatives. And on a daily basis, we condemned the various incidents that occurred. But this boiled down to reports that the HVO representatives would submit. They said that these were extreme events, extreme incidents, and this is something we had to accept because we really didn't need a second front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at the document I'm referring to now, the document under number 1. Is that a document from your brigade? Is that your document?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well, as I have already said, the brigade as such was at the forward edge facing the Serbian forces. And they were carrying out their main task, which was to prevent the Serbian forces from penetrating the municipality and town of Travnik, whereas the other men were on leave, whether on a seven-day or ten-day leave, it depended. The same people were deployed in the depth, in towns I already mentioned, in Zenica, in Travnik, in Novi Travnik, in Vitez, in Kakanj, et cetera. And I don't like to say this now, but we wrote everything down, and we from the army asked HVO members to allow those forces to pass through towards the forward edge of Defence facing our common enemy. These were requests from the operative zone of Vitez, et cetera, and here there was authorisation for passage, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to save time - and I apologise, the question will be a little leading now - is it correct to say that you have recognised this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. document as your own?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at Document Number 2. Whose document is this?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: It's from my commander of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 3. Whose document is that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: This document under number 3 is my document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 4. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is -- well, in fact, it has to do with passage of neighbouring units in the zone of my brigade. It is a request for free passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 5. Do you recognise this document dated the 25th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Again, this is from the commander of one of the battalions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 6. Do you recognise this one?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. Similarly, this is the commander of the battalion who is concerned. If I may comment, it was stating from where and how many soldiers were concerned. You know in armies, there are certain secrets about the number of men and equipment. But we were requested to provide information on the number of people who had passed through a given checkpoint. We didn't have any checkpoints. These were HVO checkpoints because they wouldn't let anyone pass through the forward edge on to Turbe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at Document Number 8. It's dated the 26th of January 1993. Is this a document that comes from a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. From the commander of the battalion again. It's interesting in that the people who were on leave would obtain wood for their houses, firewood for their houses, you know. But we also to make requests to obtain provisions for these people. And we had to make requests so that they could be allowed to pass through certain areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at the document under number 10. 28th of January is the date, the 28th of January. Do you recognise this as a document of your own? Is it a document from your brigade? And it's dated the 28th of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document of mine. I'm familiar with this document. It's also a request for free passage. It's something that occurred on a daily basis. I assume you have quite a few documents of this kind. This happened on a daily basis, and almost until June we had this task to perform. We had certain briefings with brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although you as a commander submitted a request to a military force for free passage and you had to inform of the number of men and the time at which they would be passing through, although you made these requests, were there any situations in which your soldiers were not able to reach the combat areas or reach the lines or positions where they were going?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. This would happen. How would this happen? It was a as a result of "extremist members" of the HVO and legal organs of power at the time, the HVO, said they were extremists. They said Let's go to the checkpoint, let us grant them leave to pass through. So this was really a situation that could make it go crazy. I don't know whether you have found this document or such documents, but at that time we would write to the organs of the HVO and we would say that it was pointless since we had a common enemy, and they were the Serbs. We told them it was not necessary to do what they were doing, but there were controls, and they would deprive the command of the 312th Brigade of commanders for such acts with the intent to humiliate us, and we had to keep silent. And this was because we didn't want to open a second front. We had been requested to do this. It's not something the 312th Brigade decided to do. These were political demands. They had been forwarded through the 3rd Corps command. We were requested to do all we could to avoid a conflict and to do all we could to prevent a second front from being opened. We were requested to calm the situation down and they asked us to establish a plan to avoid conflict from breaking out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, please have a look at Document Number 7. It's in the same bundle of documents. Have a look at item number 1. This is an HVO document dated the 25th of January 1993. Have a look at item number 1. Could you read it. Does what is stated under item 1 reflect the situation that you had to confront on a daily basis, that you and your soldiers had to confront on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. This is so to speak a political provocation. I haven't seen this document before. I'm reading what you referred to now, and I can only comment on what subsequently happened. Everything was done to disarm the regular army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to disarm various parts of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I rise to my feet simply for an issue of clarification. If my learned colleague is referring to Document 644, there seem to be two number 1s on that document, and she has referred the witness to number 1, and it's unclear which of those -- or perhaps I'm looking at the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. Item number 1 in the first order, which refers to the aggression of the Muslim forces. And then there is item 1 which says "completely block all movement in the area of responsibility and disarm all BH Army units and armed members." That was what the witness commented on. My question was answered by the witness, and I asked whether this order is something that he as a commander experienced on a daily basis in the area in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at number 13 now, the document under number 13. It's dated the 31st of January 1993. And this is an answer to one of your requests. Could you tell me whether you are familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document. I'm familiar with the event that is related to the request. A while ago, I mentioned the fact that we would contact directly the HVO command, and here the document has been signed by Mr. Miletic. And he said that he was -- that we should in future forward all our requests through the 3rd Corps in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, a while ago you mentioned the establishment of parallel organs of power, and you commented on a document in which it was stated that your soldiers had to fell trees in order to obtain firewood in the wintertime. Tell me, is this organ addressing you a legal organ of power, or is it some other organ of power which is preventing you from performing your duties in your very own territory?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: This is very sad. I see it now. The Croatian Community of Herceg Bosna is addressing me and giving me instructions as to what I should be doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, tell me, at some point did you as an officer and commander respond to all these humiliations?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I have already said that I responded by reporting to the command of the 3rd Corps. In view of the persistent nature of what was going on and the fact that the HVO was not allowing members of my brigade to pass through the checkpoints, I addressed the commands of the operation group I belonged to, Bugojno and Bosnian Krajina, with its headquarters in Travnik. This was set up later on in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please now look at Document Number 15 under "Movement, B."

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And after that, we will have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Is this one of the documents where you address the 3rd Corps trying to avoid any kind of conflict and asking that the corps respond to the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. This document is mine. And it reflects everything I have just said, that I addressed the command of the 3rd Corps turning to them to solve the issue of the passage of my soldiers to the zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, at your suggestion, we may take a break now. And then I will go through the remaining documents with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give you the floor, but it is quite clear that we shall not be able to finish this witness today, that we shall have to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
