utterances.text: Mr. Caber, we left off by saying that you submitted certain proposals and protests to the command of the 3rd Corps. Would you please look at Document B14, on page 2. The document is dated the 1st of February 1993. Mr. Caber, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. This was signed on my behalf by my chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, does this document correspond to what you felt as officers and human beings, and what you went through because of all the humiliation you were subjected to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: In this document, there is a description of what I have been talking about. It has to do with the passage through the HVO checkpoints. Every officer had a sense of honour, and we felt that we all belonged to the forces defending Travnik from the Serbian forces, and I was deeply insulted by all this. This is a summary report to the 3rd Corps command explaining how we felt in the brigade command at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, you also said that the political authorities and the superior military authorities demanded that you take all measures to avoid a conflict with the HVO. Would you please look at the documents under numbers 1(b), 9, and 12. In the first case, this is a document of the 27th of January 1992. It's a 3rd Corps document. The second document is also a 3rd Corps document addressed to all brigades. First, I would like to ask you, as brigade commander, did you receive this document? And does it reflect what you have just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, this certainly supports what I have said so far. The command of the 3rd Corps in all its documents and orders instructed us and ordered us to avoid conflict. They said there should not be a conflict, and that we should do everything possible to fight the common enemy together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have seen in these documents what the position of your brigade was. Could you tell Their Honours how the HVO was behaving at the time and where they set up their front lines toward the common enemy.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Starting in January when the HZHB was declared and promulgated, they insisted that -- or rather, these authorities insisted that everyone be put under HVO command. And with regard to the movements and actions of members of the HVO, we had the checkpoints we've mentioned to control movement. And these were truly unnecessary because in the situation as it was, we had sufficient strength to fend off the common enemy. And we could have done that, had we acted jointly. I'm referring to the western part of Travnik Municipality. The remaining HVO units took up positions in certain prominent facilities or areas in Travnik Municipality with certain weapons, light weapons, and also heavy weapons. They had 60- and 82-millimetre mortars, for example. When we look at Travnik Municipality, in the north, this was Karbasija; another prominent facility south of the centre of Travnik was Vilenica; and all the peripheral areas which were quite distant from the Serb forces in the Turbe area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the overall situation in the area of your brigade and your relations with the HVO, did you report regularly to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Certainly. The 3rd Corps and the operations groups, we belonged to the Operative Group West, our brigade, and because we could not communicate with them, we also communicated through the command of the 3rd Corps asking that they be informed of the situation in the brigade in the area of operations of Operational Group West which in April and May was our superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, did the command of the 3rd Corps demand of the units resubordinated to it that they should regularly, on a daily basis or at brief intervals inform them of the situation in the field, also submitting interim reports when necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As soon as the 3rd Corps was established, we were duty-bound as subordinate commands to submit reports on the situation in our units, that is, in our brigades. As soon as we had established brigades, we had to submit reports on the size and combat readiness of the brigade, and everything that affected our brigade's combat readiness. It was our duty to respond on time and to submit written reports to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, would you please look at part A, combat report, from numbers 1 to 9, and would you tell me whether you recognise these reports as reports coming from your brigade. Number 2, for example, is a report.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: We have the 3rd Corps, then we have Operative Group West, and the command of the corps received a collective report for all the brigades so that reporting was carried out in the way you have shown here. And these reports pertained to the situation in all the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3, is that your report of the 9th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 4, is this your interim report to Operative Group West?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was signed by my chief of staff, but I know about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document of the 11th of April, number 5, this is a report on the current situation.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this your document?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at Document Number 6, 7, 8, 9. Can you confirm.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: All these are combat reports, daily and interim reports. The duty to report is something that is quite normal in the military, or at least in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these reports, did you report on your relations with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: You may have noticed here that when we submit a report mentioning the Serb forces, then we include the activities of the HVO units. I reported on what HVO units were doing in the area of operations and in depth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your reports also contain information about other armed groups that may have been around or incidents that you learned had happened in the area in which your unit was deployed?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Reporting was done in the order shown here. As for incidents, let me look at this. There were quite a few incidents, especially in April 1993 when members of the HVO, on the 8th of April, put up flags of the Republic of Croatia in prominent places on government buildings. And near the building where the command of the battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was, they flew flags. On that day, Mr. Kordic visited Travnik, and this came -- this happened in the afternoon, and probably outraged by these flags, members of various brigades, including mine, took down these flags. And people who were on leave in the town did this. And that night, two of my men were killed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Who was killed?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Members of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who killed them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. There were incidents, more than one. Things really came to a head in April, in mid-April, and especially in May, in the peripheral Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. parts of the municipality, especially in Kalibunar when members of the HVO insisted that all armed formations should be put under their command. This is in addition to what I mentioned happened in January, and that Muslim citizens should move out of certain buildings in the local community of Kalinar, and this was all at the first line of defence, 5 or 6 kilometres away from the first line of defence facing the Serb forces. And all this indicated a growing problem for the 312th Brigade of the army. We had to calm people down, sit down round a table and talk to avoid a conflict. And the men at the first line of defence were outraged, and I had certain problems in keeping them from returning to the town of Travnik and the villages to defend their families. These are reports mentioning all the things I'm saying now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although two members of your brigade were killed on the 8th of April, you say that you organised meetings, you pleaded that a conflict be avoided. How did the HVO behave and how did they respond to your efforts to avoid a conflict? Were there any movements of the HVO forces in the town or outside the town? Did anything else happen that might help us assess the situation in which you found yourself in April and May?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: As I have already said, we had frequent meetings with HVO commanders. The HVO authorities and the legitimate municipal authorities held meetings to avoid a conflict. They kept saying that these were extremists and that they should be removed, that we should act together to get rid of extremists, and they were simply paying lip service to our joint efforts. But then the same things would happen over and over again on the ground. The HVO units were already engaging in combat in certain villages, and again, they were saying that these were just extremists, renegades who were out of control. This happened in Kalibunar. That was a local commune. And they were already taking up positions in certain facilities and prominent features with weapons. And their actions were not aimed at what we were talking about, jointly fighting the common enemy. It's true that they had some hundred men in the area of the village of Dijace fending off the Serb forces. But all their remaining forces were in the rear and had different tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, was there at one point fighting in the town itself, and was there any movement of the population out of the town? If so, what were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: In early June, there were already certain movements of HVO units, provocations at the checkpoints, and armed incidents which grew into an armed conflict. As far as I can recall, on the 3rd of June in the afternoon, there was an incident in the neighbourhood of Slimene, which is to the southeast of the centre of town. And the -- and some members of the HVO demanded that in a certain area where the majority population was Croat, there Muslims should move out. All the members of the army who were then on leave and all those who had connections to the area opposed this, and armed incidents occurred. From the 3rd of June onwards, incidents took place daily. Or better to say, armed clashes. And this led to daily meetings, negotiations, and talks at the highest levels, military and political, in order to stop this. However, these clashes did not stop, and they took a course that was very unfortunate for everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, to return to another topic, we have talked about the problems you encountered in establishing your brigade, in your relations with the HVO, and the outbreak of an open conflict. Tell me now, did the command of the 3rd Corps take certain measures, issue certain orders, or do anything else to transfer to you certain powers and authorities in order that you might set up your unit under these difficult circumstances as a disciplined military unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Mr. President, that's a leading question, and it's also a compound question. There's several different parts of that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will put a few simple questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question contains eight lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take any steps under these difficult circumstances to make your brigade a disciplined military brigade? And what measures did you take?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I have already spoken of the difficulties in establishing the brigade, but in order to have a good military unit, even in peacetime, let alone during war, discipline and order have to be very strong from the top down. We carried out all these activities in the complex situation we were in. We did this on the ground in direct contact with individuals, with commanders, and at times of rest or change of shift. I would address the men personally and draw their attention to the necessity of implementing all military disciplinary regulations. I would inform them of the overall situation, both political and military, and I always stressed very strongly that a soldier must respect certain duties and obligations when carrying weapons and in combat; that they had to preserve their own lives, the lives of their comrades, the lives of citizens, and the property of citizens if they were located in the combat zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, did you receive any orders or instructions to this effect from the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Everything I've just mentioned was pursuant to the instructions and commands of the command of the 3rd Corps and their orders. And the members of the command of the 3rd Corps visited us to see to what extent we were implementing their orders and the code of conduct I've just described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at Document Number 3 and Document Number 4 and tell me whether this is one of the orders issued by the 3rd Corps drawing attention to the necessity. It's number 1. I apologise, it's number 1, Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the parts I'm referring to are 4 and 3. 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is issued by the Ministry of Defence, and it's number 0606, Defence number, and the document of the 22nd of January 1993, command of the 3rd Corps, Defence number 0613. This is the first part entitled "BH Army." Have you found these two documents?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise these documents as ones you received from the 3rd Corps, and are these some of the orders and documents you received at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly. This is signed by Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic. It refers to disciplinary responsibility, and so on. I remember these instructions well. And pursuant to this, at our own level, we elaborated on all this. And as for the rules on military discipline, we elaborated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, as a commander, were you authorised to pronounce disciplinary measures against your men, and did you do so for breaches of discipline or other offences committed by your men?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. For misdemeanors that were not so serious, I was authorised to do that. In cases of serious breaches of discipline, I would have to refer those to the command of the 3rd Corps. I don't remember if there were any such cases, but this order I'm looking at now, I remember that we did implement it, that we complied with it, we acted on it. And all those who violated military discipline were punished either by detention or certain other measures. Sometimes due to the combat situation, simply talking to a soldier was a good measure, if that can be considered punishment. That was one of the milder punishments, just a talk with him. Sometimes a soldier would refuse to go to the front line because his family had nothing to eat or because he was afraid because of the vicinity of the HVO to where his family was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, are you aware that a decree was issued regulating the establishment of special courts? And did you have any orders pertaining to this from the 3rd Corps? And as brigade commander, did you act in compliance with such orders, if there were any?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well, look. In 1992, or rather the end of 1992 and in 1993, I do remember such orders, and I understood them correctly, orders on the creation of special military courts. And the purpose of them was primarily to deal with a lack of discipline within brigades, within our ranks. And as a result of such an order, I did establish a special military court. What is more, I was also supposed to put it into function because of the lack of discipline of certain individuals and of units, too. I was aware of this, of the existence of such a body, and it did operate within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, as a commander, did you at any time receive an order from the 3rd Corps command relating to the application of the Geneva Convention and of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I can't remember. But as I said a minute ago, as a former professional member of the military, I was familiar with the decrees, with the principles, with the importance of the Geneva Convention. And similarly, we were constantly receiving certain documents. But I shouldn't omit to say that given that I was familiar with the 3rd Corps and that they were professional, I'm sure that they forwarded such instructions. I must have received something to that effect, and I attempted to ensure that the Geneva Conventions were respected. And I attempted to ensure that officers, commanders of battalions, of companies and of platoons were fully aware and implemented the rules. All of our members had served in the former JNA, and I know that when I was a member of the former JNA this was a subject that was obligatory for all soldiers. So this was just a matter of reminding men of these conventions, because in the former JNA a lot of attention was paid to these matters. Yet, some people do forget about them, and it's necessary to remind them. But each soldier, each officer was obliged to abide by what was internationally recognised and was obliged to conduct themselves in accordance with these principles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at documents under 21 and 22 in the first section. But first of all, I would like to ask you whether you received any orders relating to the protection of civilians, the protection of property. And did you take any measures in order to ensure that civilians and property were protected?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well, as I said a minute ago, I won't go into where this order came from, but the month is June 1993. It's the beginning of June. And in certain circumstances - and we know under what circumstances - the Croatian people left its villages in the depth, as you look at them from the front line of defence in the direction of the Serbian forces, those villages remained without any protection. No Croatian inhabitants remained in them with the exception of a few of the inhabitants. Some of them did remain in the villages. And the property in these villages, the houses, had to be secured. They had to be protected. The depth concerned was very deep, so we're talking about the Municipality of Travnik and the centre as far as Turbe. That's about 7 or 8 kilometres. And all the villages there were Croatian villages. It was necessary to secure a number of villages. The area was a vast area, and it was necessary to issue orders. It was necessary to ensure that the organs of military security and that the organs of military police provided security to the highest possible level for those villages. And it was necessary to make sure they provided security for the inhabitants. But we also had contacts with the organs of legal power at the time, with the president of the municipal assembly. We had contact with the civil protection as well. Again, this relates to the organs of power. And we had contact with the Ministry of the Interior, and attempts were made to secure the abandoned villages and to protect them. What I'm trying to say is that measures were taken in order to prevent anything from being done that might be a violation of the Geneva Conventions, in order to prevent anarchy, in order to prevent looting, et cetera, et cetera. We made such attempts. I'm not saying that we provided a hundred per cent security, but we -- in the villages Pirota, Sipovik, Vidosevici, Kokosari, Visokovici, Miskina Brdo, Kraljevica, Pesevici and Pirici, and these are large, very pretty villages, they're nice villages to live in in the Municipality of Travnik, these are villages that remained abandoned and we tried to protect them and to prevent them from being torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, you have commented on these documents. And a minute ago you said that if soldiers violated those orders and those instructions, in such cases you would take disciplinary measures. Were there any other measures you took against these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well look, by all means. When the court was established, the judicial authorities were active in the Municipality of Travnik, and my security organ was active, the commander was active. And via the military police, we attempted to deal with all violations. And if we're talking about these Croatian villages which were in the depth of the brigade where there was ongoing combat, we attempted to protect, to secure these villages. Any violations were qualified as crimes, and we would forward such cases to the court. I have mentioned there were quite a lot of reports which we would forward to the court. There were quite a lot of criminal reports. I no longer remember what the court did, but I know that a fair number of my men were referred to the court. They were put on trial. I can no longer remember how they were punished, but there are quite a lot of proceedings instituted because of looting, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, have a look at the document, the same document, and have a look at item number 12. Have a look at the document number 12 in the same section. This document is dated the 2nd of May 1993. And I would like to ask you whether this is a document from your brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. This is the command of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what he represents.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well, he represents what I've just been talking about. It has to do with all those criminal cases that were instituted against members of my brigade. And the reasons that are contained in this document are before you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date of this report is the 2nd of May. And if I can see this correctly, by that time, your military police had filed criminal reports against 61 soldiers. A minute ago, you said that there were far more criminal reports that were filed after the Croatian population left the areas in the immediate vicinity of Travnik in June.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have I understood your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, I would now like to ask you the following: In order to conclude my examination and allow the Prosecution and Judges to ask you questions tomorrow, could you please have a look at other documents in section 1, have a look at documents 1 to 26. After you have had a look at them, could you tell me whether these are documents from your brigade, or rather whether these are documents which demonstrate the kind of measures taken by your brigade. Take your time to have a look at each document. If there are any that you cannot identify, feel free to say so.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I don't know if it's necessary for me to comment on all of these documents, on what is stated in the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you think that you would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to one of the documents, please do so. But first of all, I would like to know whether you recognise these documents, whether you could say that these are documents that you or your units drafted or they are documents you received from superior commands. Or are they criminal reports that you filed against members of your units? If after you have examined the documents from 1 to 26 you see there are some that you can't identify as one that you drafted, received, or sent to someone, I'd be grateful if you could mention the fact.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: All these documents come from the brigade, and they reflect the situation such as it was. Many of them are documents that I signed, and others were signed by my assistants, assistants for security, for example. And there are some documents that arrived from the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we just have a look at Document Number 19, and could you tell me, since you have said that this is a document from your unit, could you tell me whether this is a document that, in fact, is a good reflection of what you have testified about before this Trial Chamber. And it is a document on some of the measures that you took to ensure that there was discipline in the army and to ensure that the army rules and regulations were respected.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Yes. This is a true reflection of everything that I have already stated. The subject itself of the document has to do with maintaining order and discipline amongst conscripts in populated areas and towns. There are ten items under the order, and all these items reflect that fact. I don't think it's necessary to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, I only have another three brief questions. You have told us about the kind of brigade you had at the beginning. You told us about the equipment you had to start off with. And in spite of all these efforts, given all of these efforts you had to make, can you tell me what your brigade looked like towards the end of 1993 and to what extent were you able to transform this brigade into one that resembled a brigade in the JNA? And you were a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: Well, given the time, the situation was such that in those years, in the 1990s, it was my task to -- or in 1990, it was my task to form an armoured battalion in the JNA. I wasn't able to carry out this task in one year. But I had all the men and all the equipment in an area of about 500 square kilometres. I wasn't able to carry out this task to form a brigade. Well, forming a brigade is a very big and responsible task. I accepted this task only because I felt the need to be in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I returned to be in Bosnia and Herzegovina with citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina who belonged to all the ethnic communities. I returned to form a brigade which would be composed of members of all the ethnic groups. However, I have already spoken about what happened. And to my great joy, there were some members of other ethnic groups who remained in my brigade. There were Serbs and Croats who occupied key positions in the brigade command or in the battalions, and my officers were also professional. But now from this viewpoint, I would say that the brigade I had wasn't organised in the way it should have been organised in order to carry out all its duties assigned to it by the superior command. In 1992, in 1993, given all the problems, given the refugees, given the presence of a lot of commands, communications units, et cetera, given the widespread hunger, it was difficult to form and establish a brigade, a brigade which was operational, mobile, and ready to carry out tasks. The brigade that I had was equipped, and it had been trained to protect the area in which it was present. I mentioned the line in the Turbe zone of responsibility, and in my opinion the brigade managed to carry out that task. But as to whether it was a brigade -- well, perhaps there was a battalion that was sufficiently armed. Perhaps the brigade had the weapons a battalion would have. But the fact that it had 3.000 men, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Caber, as a professional officer, you speak about that period as a professional officer. Given the circumstances that prevailed - given the fact that two wars were being waged, there were refugees, there was widespread hunger, there was a lack of weapons - do you believe that you did whatever you could, and do you believe that the officers did everything they could given the circumstances at the time? Was everything done as far as forming that brigade is concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: I think that I did everything that I could, everything that a man could possibly do. I also had my family in Travnik. But believe me, sometimes I wouldn't even be able to visit them for a 15-day period. It was necessary to examine the entire situation, to protect the area. But there were a lot of shortcomings. It was very difficult, it really was. But as I say, I don't think we did enough. As to why, this is a subject that should be discussed at some other time. But to form a brigade in such conditions and in such surroundings was difficult. We carried out the task as far as protecting the municipality is concerned. But as to whether we did everything we could do, as to we could have done more, well, we probably could have but I think we probably did the maximum. Officers did what they could to the extent that they were able to cooperating with the organs of power. There was the HVO. There were the legal authorities, et cetera. The troops were hungry and were without weapons, were without equipment, and didn't have any provisions for their family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. Caber: You were an officer in the BH Army. And in 1993, you were in hotspots in the battlefield. Could you tell me whether your brigade or whether parts of the brigade at any time attacked Croatian villages, occupied or conquered other people's territory?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER
utterances.text: No. The brigade as such, and given the situation it was in, it was facing the Serbian forces, the brigade's main task was always to protect and to provide security for the citizens, regardless of their nationality. This was their task in the Municipality of Travnik and in the zone in which we operated. I have indicated this zone to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Caber. Mr. President, this concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will Mr. Kubura's Defence team have any questions for this witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis, how much time do you think you will require.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will certainly assess the situation overnight, but I would not imagine that I would need more than 45 minutes to one hour. Perhaps 90 minutes, but I can't imagine going over one court session, and probably half to two-thirds of a court session will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're a little late because the second witness was going to be heard over two days, and the third one on Friday. So we should try to shorten the examination of the second witness, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we said that we would organise the examination in such a way that we can finish examining these witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, Mr. Caber, you'll have to return tomorrow. You shouldn't see anyone until then because you've taken the solemn declaration, and you're testifying in the interests of justice. Have a good evening, and I invite you to return tomorrow for the hearing that will commence at 2.15. The usher will now escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the witness with regard to which we have rendered a decision, as one says, you can sleep on it. You will have the time to think about it, and we will discuss the issue tomorrow. It is now 7.00, and I will see everyone at the hearing tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
